en: Śrī.

The *Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya*, one of the fundamental root-texts composed by the venerable Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. Salutations to Śrī Lakṣmī-Hayagrīva, who is the essence of Śrīmat Hanumat, Bhīma, Madhva, Antargata Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and Vedavyāsa.

In the first chapter: I ever revere Nārāyaṇa, who is to be known solely through the true scriptures, who has transcended both the perishable and the imperishable, and whose excellent qualities are beyond all description.
Those specific qualities which have been described here through well-spoken words,
I shall establish them in due order for the understanding of the virtuous.
The Ṛgveda and the others, the Bhārata, the entire Pañcarātra,
the original Rāmāyaṇa, and the Purāṇas— all these consist of that very essence.
And all those who follow them are always in accordance with the sacred scriptures;
Janārdana cannot be known by others than those who are difficult to master.
"He is to be known by those who are always disciplined, devoted, and firmly established;
not by mere logic, nor by that which is born of the senses, nor by anything else.
He is to be known through scripture alone by devotees, and not otherwise. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa*.
"One who does not know the Veda does not comprehend that Great One, the Self who is experienced as all, at the time of passing away"—so says the Taittirīya Śruti.
"This understanding is not to be attained through reasoning; it must be declared by another for the sake of right knowledge, O dearest one."
Moreover, there is the Kaṭha-śruti:
"Neither the senses nor inference [know Him]; the Vedas alone cause one to know Him; therefore they say, 'the Vedas.
And there is the Pippalāda-śruti: "The Vedas indeed cause one to know Him."
Nor is there a lack of authority in these very words, because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), and because [the Purāṇas] are included therein, as it is said:

"Itihāsa and Purāṇa are the fifth Veda among the Vedas. Nor should it be argued that there is no such thing as a sentence that is not of human origin; for if such were absent, the Dharma and other principles accepted by all philosophical systems would remain unestablished. One who does not accept those two [Dharma and Adharma] is not a follower of a system (*samayin*), because he lacks the purpose for a system. Furthermore, there can be no benefit to the world through him, since the absence of Dharma and so forth leads only to mutual injury and the like. Nor does he have any purpose in providing benefit, because there is no unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) resulting from it.

Therefore, by one who asserts the non-existence of dharma and so forth, the futility of their own system is effectively admitted; thus, such a person is not a follower of that system. Nor can its establishment be achieved through a human statement, because [in that case] ignorance or deception would be possible. Furthermore, an omniscient being cannot be postulated for the sake of that [human statement], because this would entail the burden of multiple assumptions: the assumption of omniscience—which has never been observed elsewhere—the assumption of his non-deceptiveness, and the assumption that he composed that [statement].

If one accepts that the Vedic sentences are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), nothing further need be postulated. Furthermore, their lack of human authorship is established by itself, because no author of the Vedas is known. Since no such author is known, to postulate one would involve the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). On the other hand, if one does not postulate an author, the fact of its being authorless is established as a matter of course. Nor can it be said that the Vedas have an author like worldly sentences, for there is no established tradition regarding such an author. Nor has anyone stated that "the Veda was made by someone," as there is an absence of any such lineage of transmission.

Nor does a statement not seen by the seers of the Vedas become a Vedic sentence merely because they have spontaneously manifested the Vedas; for [the Vedas] are governed by sentences established through tradition, and because those seers of the Vedas are themselves devoid of faults. And it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*:

"One who possesses ascetic power, knows many Vedas, and is not deficient in the twenty characteristics—whoever should regard him as 'the Veda' himself on account of his vision of knowledge, he is the Veda."

Validity (*prāmāṇya*) is indeed intrinsic (*svataḥ*), for otherwise there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is validity dependent upon the aforementioned reasoning (*yukti*), because reasonings serve only to eliminate defects in cognition, and validity is established intrinsically for those whose cognitions are free from defects. Nor should it be argued that there is no infinite regress because one depends on another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) only when there is a desire for further inquiry (*ākāṅkṣā*); for such a desire itself consists in a defect of cognition. Since doubt regarding invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) arises only in the case of defective cognitions, invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*), while validity is established intrinsically.

Nor should it be said that the production of phonemes occurs only at the time of their utterance, for that would contradict the recognition (pratyabhijñā) that "this very same word is that [same word]. Nor should it be argued that this recognition is an error due to similarity, for then even such recognitions as "this is that Devadatta" would likewise have to be considered erroneous. Furthermore, if the Buddhist were to claim that all things are momentary, they could not then maintain that recognitions such as "this is that same direction" are non-erroneous, since [the subject] would be distinct from the five aggregates (pañcaskandha).

Nor are the directions themselves merely imagined through delusion, for there is a parity between consciousness (*vijñāna*) and emptiness (*śūnya*). Nor is the conceptualization of direction dependent solely on the rising of the sun and so forth, since the mere perception of direction occurs even in darkness. It is only an occasional delusion that is removed by the observation of the rising of the sun and such; and that [delusion] occurs even in the case of consciousness and emptiness—such is their view, due to the disagreement among disputants. Therefore, it is established that the directions are indeed stable, just like emptiness. Consequently, the stability of the Veda is likewise established, because of the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) that "this very same sentence is this."

Furthermore, inference and other means of knowledge do not possess validity regarding dharma and such matters in the absence of scripture, because those [means] do not have such things as their domain.

Therefore, since dharma and so forth are established only by means of impersonal (apauruṣeya) speech, all disputants must accept that [scripture]. And its validity is established intrinsically (svataḥ). If one does not accept that invalidity is extrinsic (parataḥ), then even defective sense organs and the like could not be the cause of invalidity. And if that were not accepted, it would contradict experience. Thus, it is established that validity is intrinsic and invalidity is extrinsic.
"O Virūpa, with speech that is eternal and with that which is both eternal and non-eternal, I praise that supreme state, Brahman.
"The Vedas are indeed eternal, while the Smṛtis and other speeches are non-eternal."
Thus says the Paiṅgi-Śruti:
"The supreme Brahman is that which is to be known; the supreme Śruti is that which makes it known. It is beginningless and eternal, and without that [Śruti], it cannot be attained."
Thus says the Kātyāyana Śruti:
"A thousandfold are its greatnesses; as far as the Brahman extends, so far extends speech.
What wise man has truly known the application of the meters? Who has attained the responsive word of the sacrificial hearths?"
And thus:
"The Vedas in their entirety are eternal and perpetual, residing within the intellect of Viṣṇu;
in every creation, they are uttered by him in that very same manner."
They must be produced by those very syllables and those very vowels in that specific sequence, and not otherwise;
for this reason they are called *śrutis*, since they have been heard (*śruta*) by all.
Indeed, they were heard in a previous birth through the grace of Vāsudeva.
They will appear to the sages only in part, and not in their entirety.
Since they were seen by Hari and heard by other people,
they are called "Śrutis" (the heard) and "Dṛṣṭis" (the seen) by the ancients.
And the statement regarding its arising would indeed be dependent upon manifestation,
just as the birth of a conscious being is spoken of by all worldly people.
The Purāṇas, which have those same meanings, are indeed composed differently in each creation; therefore, they are non-eternal, yet their meanings remain as they were in previous creations.

"The creation-passages of the Vedas may be [understood] with reference to individual [manifestations], or with reference to the gods who possess intermediate presiding powers (abhimānin). How could there be impermanence for those whose nature is eternal? For they are stable. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
Furthermore, specific terms such as "the Veda is heard" (*śruti*) and so forth would not be appropriate if [the Veda] were impermanent;

for those Vedas are eternal because they are known by all, and because they are heard by everyone. Tradition (*āmnāya*) is never otherwise recited, as it has always resided within the intellect of the Lord.
Thus it is stated in the *Mahāvārāha*.

Furthermore, the empirical usage of the Vedas would not be tenable without their eternity. Nor is it proper to assert that phonemes, words, and so forth are non-eternal, because they are perceived at all times within the cognition of the Lord, who is the proponent of omniscience. Nor is it proper to assert that they are mere mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) like a jar or other objects, because the contradiction with recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has already been stated. Nor is it proper to assert that they are mere mental impressions like a jar or other objects, because the contradiction with recognition has already been stated. Even in the case of the Purāṇas, non-eternality consists merely in the composition of words in a different manner.
Therefore, it is established that the phonemes (*varṇa*) and so forth manifested in sound—which is a quality of space—and the Veda, which consists of their sequence, are indeed eternal.

Nor is there invalidity [of a word] on the grounds that it lacks linguistic usage (*vyutpatti*) regarding an already established (*siddha*) object; for linguistic usage is grasped precisely with respect to an established object as related to another. Indeed, in cases such as "This is your mother" or "This is your father," one learns that meaning only through an instruction preceded by gestures such as pointing a finger. For one who asserts that linguistic usage occurs only with respect to what is related to a task (*kāryānvita*), there is the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*), because a task cannot be related to itself. This is because in instances such as "This is your mother," "This is your father," or "You are handsome," the sentence concludes simply by making known an established fact.

This is because its authority is experienced there [in that context]. Furthermore, there is no purpose for a sentence other than making known what is already established; for it is only by knowing that something is a means to a desired end that one engages in action, and conversely, one desists from it when the opposite is known. Therefore, the authority of all sentences is established as being directed toward what is already established. Moreover, it is well-known and accepted by all disputants that grammar, etymology (*nirukta*), and so forth, possess authority only regarding what is already established. If this were not admitted, all linguistic usage would fail to be established. As it is said in the *Nāradīya*:
"To Nārāyaṇa, the omniscient, the creator of all, who is free from affliction..."
For here they indeed declare the supreme among all things, the great ultimate intent.
"For all the Vedas, for the Itihāsas and Purāṇas,
and for all means of valid knowledge, that [ultimate goal] is stated as their purpose."

Furthermore, the non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) is not established; thus, the statements regarding difference are merely reiterative (*anuvāda*). Without scripture (*āgama*), the Lord himself is not established. Nor can he be established through inference (*anumāna*), because an inference could just as well be made to the contrary. When it is argued, "The subject of dispute has a creator, because it is an effect, like a pot," one may counter with the opposing inference: "The subject of dispute has no creator, because it lacks a creator as accepted by us, like the self (*ātman*). If it is argued that "non-being-an-effect" is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), then we reply that "being produced by one possessing a body" is equally an adjunct in the other case.

Furthermore, since difference is established through perception and inference, the scripture teaching non-difference is invalid precisely because it contradicts them. Therefore, insofar as this scripture of non-difference lacks invalidity, the statements regarding difference cannot be considered mere restatements (*anuvādaka*). For that which is stronger is not a restatement, as it serves as a cause for strengthening [the truth].

Even though scripture possesses greater authority than perception and the like, it does not possess validity when it contradicts a foundational means of knowledge (*upajīvya-pramāṇa*), because in the absence of an object, its own invalidity would follow. Indeed, even in that [Advaita] position, the object of scripture is established by that very same inference and so forth.

For, according to the view that [the scripture] merely restates what is established by inference, God is to be known through inference, while the scripture is to be known through perception. Therefore, in the event of a contradiction between these two, there would be no authoritative validity. Furthermore, the distinction from the God established by inference is established by direct experience itself, because the individual soul (jīva) is experienced as not being the creator of all. Nor can the scripture possess authoritative validity when it contradicts direct experience; for if the scripture were authoritative, it would follow that the experience itself lacks authority. Moreover, agreement with many means of knowledge is indeed a cause of firmness, since firmness is observed precisely in the case of multiple witnesses stating the same thing.

Only in cases where there is universal non-disagreement can there be any semblance of restatement (*anuvādakatva*). However, there is no such universal non-disagreement here, as we observe disagreement regarding [the nature of] oneness and so forth. Furthermore, when there is a conflict with many means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the invalidity of a single one is observed, as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like. Nor is it the case that weakness arises solely from being produced by a defect (*doṣa*); rather, there is a contradiction [in your position], because it is a rule that those things contradicted by many means of valid cognition are necessarily produced by defects. Moreover, the fact of being produced by a defect is known precisely from the contradiction with a stronger means of valid cognition. [Thus: "The sense organ is unimpaired; likewise, reasoning (*tarka*) and inference (*anumā*) are unimpaired."
Āgama is the word of one who is not corrupt; and self-evident testimony (svadṛgvākya) is considered to be direct experience (anubhava).
Faults are to be understood through a stronger means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not otherwise;
and this strength is twofold: by way of multiplicity and by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Between these two, the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is stronger, as it is that which is dependent upon [the object] and so forth;
validity is indeed conformity with reality (yāthārthya), and that is the primary [meaning] of the words "knowledge" and "word."
Knowledge is of two kinds: external and likewise that which consists of internal experience.
Among these, experience is like strength; therein, that which arises from the senses and so forth is faultless.
Consequently, the triad beginning with perception (akṣa) attains the status of being subordinate;
thus, the inherent superiority of scripture alone is traditionally held among those three.
However, when there is a contradiction with that upon which it depends, this [scripture] possesses no authority.
Some call inference (anumā) that which consists of the parts [of a syllogism], such as the proposition and so forth;
however, that is useless, for even that does not attain the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) without logical justification.
Therefore, reasoning alone is the means of valid cognition consisting of inference;
and reasoning takes the form of a proposition, as well as the forms of a reason and an example.

Likewise, the other [member] consisting of application (upanaya) and that which consists of the conclusion (nigamana) each attain the status of a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) precisely through their logical necessity;
for the proposition (*pratijñā*), being pregnant with the reason (*hetu*), will likewise attain separate authority.
If the reason were established as something separate from the thesis, it would be a distinct means of valid cognition;
however, because it is a constituent part of the thesis, its status as a means of valid cognition exists only through independence [from the thesis].
The example proceeds merely by relying upon pervasion (*vyāpti*), while the application (*upanaya*) likewise relies solely on pervasion;
yet even pervasion alone may constitute a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it is based on a necessary rule (*niyama*).
Likewise, the conclusion (nigamana), by virtue of its singular nature as a summary, attains validity;
experience makes known its status as a logical justification.
Contradiction, as well as excess, deficiency, and inconsistency—these should be understood as defects of reasoning; and contradiction is internal by its very nature.
For Janaka, transgression would result in birth, whether for himself or for another.
A means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is defined as that which brings about the manifestation of its own object.
These very same [points] would constitute defeats when combined with the failure to respond to the challenge.
In its essential sense, presumption (arthāpatti) is defined as the very act of postulation;
it occurs when, having perceived something similar, one infers a previously seen object.
The cognition of similarity to this [perceived object] is proclaimed as analogy (upamāna).
The thorough knowledge of non-existence (abhāva) is declared to be of two kinds.
Among those, one is for the practitioner who experiences [the object] through non-perception;
the second is to be understood as applying to pleasure and so forth, as well as to jars and the like.
One [type of non-existence] is of the nature of perception, while the second consists of inference;
in some cases, even the absence of a jar or similar object is apprehended through perception.
Because it is understood instantaneously, it is not considered to arise from a logical mark (liṅga).
Arthāpatti and upamāna are indeed merely varieties of inference. Scripture (āgama) should be known as being of two kinds: eternal and likewise non-eternal.

Perception is considered to be threefold: that which pertains to the knower, that which pertains to the object of knowledge, and that which pertains to the Lord; likewise, it is of two kinds—natural (yaugika) and non-natural (ayaugika)—and is essentially of the nature of direct experience.
The senses are their own essential forms and consist of eternal consciousness;
likewise, those of Viṣṇu and Śrī are said to be so, while those of others are of two kinds.
Their individual forms are distinct and of three kinds:
those of the gods, those of the asuras, and those that are intermediate; this has been declared through direct perception.
Indeed, a sense organ (akṣa) that is directed toward objects is celebrated as "perception" (pratyakṣa);
however, the sense organ of the Person (puruṣa), which is imperishable, is primary in its own essential nature.
The term "metaphorical designation" (upacāra) applies elsewhere because there is an accumulation [of parts] in that creation;
inference and the like are so called because their nature is that of logical proof (upapatti).

"Through the greatness of direct perception and scripture, inference attains the status of a valid means of knowledge; otherwise, its necessity could never be established anywhere. Thus it is said in the *Brahmatarka*.

In this context, since the means of knowledge (*pramā*) that serves as the basis for reliance is stronger, it is logical that the intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies precisely in difference (*bheda*). Furthermore, how could there be the status of a restatement (*anuvādakatva*) regarding difference if it has not been established by a means of valid cognition? And if it is already established, how could a statement of non-difference (*abheda*) sublate it? Nor does a means of valid cognition become a restatement on the basis of something established by what is not a means of valid cognition. Moreover, if [the means of knowledge] were weak, the cognition of difference would be fallacious, and thus the statements of difference would not possess the status of restatement. Therefore, the statements of difference alone possess greater force.

If one were to accept the superiority of statements that contradict all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then since the meanings perceived without inquiry in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed nothing at all; from non-being, being was born" would themselves contradict all *pramāṇas*, it would follow that the primary purport (*mahātātparya*) of all the scriptures lies therein.

Nor should it be said that there is a contradiction with reason (*yukti*) in that case; for on that view, the fact that [the scripture] does not merely restate what is already established by reason would itself be a merit. Indeed, it would only be a restatement if it were already established by reason. Therefore, since there is no restatement when [the matter] is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), nor when it is established by reason—which is not a valid means of knowledge—there is no weakness in the statements concerning difference.

Nor does the multiplicity of means of knowledge (pramāṇa) entail weakness; indeed, firmness is observed precisely when there is corroboration by multiple statements. If that were not the case, even repetition and the like would become causes for invalidity. Furthermore, it is established for everyone that repetition is an indicator of the speaker's intention (tātparya). If this were not admitted, then even in your own position, the statement "That thou art" repeated nine times would lack authority because it would be a mere restatement due to such repetition.

When it is argued that the first statement alone would be insufficient and thus another is required, the reply is that the second statement is for the sake of one by whom the distinction [of Viṣṇu] has not been ascertained through perception and other means. Therefore, strength lies precisely in the corroboration of many means of knowledge.

Consequently, because it would contradict all means of knowledge, the sentence does not have non-difference as its purport; rather, the great purport of all the Āgamas is simply the supremacy of Viṣṇu.
And so it was said by the Blessed One:
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
The perishable consists of all beings, while the one who stands at the peak is called the imperishable.
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is designated as the Supreme Self;
the immutable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them.
Since I transcend the perishable and am even superior to the imperishable, [I am the highest].
Therefore, I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama.
He who, undeluded, thus knows Me as Puruṣottama— he, O Bhārata, knowing Me as the All-Knowing, worships Me with his whole being.
"Thus, O sinless one, this most secret teaching has been declared by me;
having understood this, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done, O Bhārata.
Thus [it is said]. In the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, there is no great reality whatsoever other than Him.
That devotion to that [ultimate goal] is the intermediate aim; all other scriptures have that as their purpose, for the human goal arises from it.
Thus says the Paiṅgi-Śruti.

"The primary purport of all the Vedas is the supreme excellence of the Lord of Śrī; whereas their purport regarding anything other than that would be secondary. Thus it is stated in the Mahāvarāha [Purāṇa].
And it is logical that the great purport of all the Āgamas is precisely the supreme excellence of Viṣṇu.

"For liberation is indeed the highest of all human goals; dharma, artha, and kāma are all impermanent, whereas liberation alone is eternal. Therefore, a wise man should strive for its sake. Thus says the Bhāllaveya Śruti.

"Because they are impermanent and characterized by suffering, phenomena (*dharma*) and the like are not the supreme bliss; liberation alone is the supreme joy for those wandering in *saṃsāra*. Thus it is said in the *Mahābhārata*. Furthermore, liberation is not obtained without the grace of Viṣṇu.
By whose grace one is liberated from this saṃsāra, which consists of supreme suffering, and not by any other—
He is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme, who should be meditated upon by those seeking liberation from these bonds of karma.
And thus says the Nārāyaṇa-śruti:
"This Self is not to be grasped by instruction, nor by intellect, nor by much hearing.
Only he whom this [Self] chooses, by him is it attained; to him this Self reveals its own form."
Thus says the Kaṭha Śruti.
I become their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence,
O Pārtha, without delay, for those whose minds are absorbed in Me.
Thus says the Blessed One: "Since origination, maintenance, and dissolution, destiny, ignorance, and obscuration,
as well as bondage and liberation, proceed from the Person (Puruṣa), He is Hari, the sole sovereign."
Thus it is said in the Skanda Purāṇa:
"To the ignorant, Viṣṇu is the destroyer of the defects of ignorance; to the wise, he is the giver of liberation;
and to those who are liberated, he alone is Janārdana, the bestower of bliss. And also: [as stated above].

"He is the binder by the noose of worldly existence and the liberator from the noose of worldly existence; he is the bestower of absolute liberation, the Supreme Brahman—Viṣṇu himself, there is no doubt. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, affection arises specifically from the knowledge of the excellence of qualities, not from the knowledge of non-difference. Indeed, for the noble-minded, non-difference leads only to displeasure; for kings cause those who say "I am the king" to be executed, yet they grant everything desired to one who speaks of the excellence of their qualities.
The kind of joy one feels toward the praiseworthy Viṣṇu when recognizing the excellence of his qualities cannot be matched by any other.
Through pleasing Him, one attains liberation; therefore, all the Vedas are entirely devoted to that.
Thus says the Śruti of Suparṇa:
"O Bhārata, he who, undeluded, knows me thus as the Supreme Person— he, knowing all, worships me with his whole being."

Thus, the Blessed One himself has declared that supreme love arises solely from the knowledge of the excellence of His qualities. Therefore, the primary purport of all the Śrutis and Smṛtis is precisely the excellence of Viṣṇu’s qualities;
there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that their purport lies in non-duality.

Nor is difference established through the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya*). The state of being qualifier and qualified depends upon difference. Difference is established in dependence upon the substratum (*dharmin*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), and the status of being a substratum or a counter-correlate depends upon difference; thus, because of this mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), difference is untenable. This is because difference is the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity. Nor is difference non-intrinsic (*asvarūpa*) in dependence upon the substratum and the counter-correlate, for like unity, it is precisely the intrinsic nature that exists in such a manner.

Furthermore, for one who asserts the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*), the establishment of their essential nature (*svarūpasiddhi*) is already established. Distinction (*bheda*), however, is established only upon the perception of that essential nature—just as it is said that the essential nature of an object is generally distinct from everything else. If distinction were not the essential nature, then when an object is perceived, its general distinction from all other things would not be known. And if that distinction were unknown, there would even be doubt whether "this is a pot" or "this is the Self. Yet no one entertains such a doubt.

Having generally cognized the distinctness [of an object] from everything else, one entertains doubt only regarding something that is similar; for no one ever has a doubt such as "Am I Devadatta or not? regarding the self. Only when the general distinctness from all things is known does the cognition of "pot-ness" and so forth arise. Therefore, there is no circularity (*anyonyāśrayatā*).

Nor is the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions a defect. Just as when one perceives a thousand lamps simultaneously, they are all known in their general aspect, so it would be here. Furthermore, even those [who hold the Advaita view] must admit distinctions regarding a single object, because in the statement "not this, not this" (*neti neti*), a distinction from everything else is admitted. Moreover, if no distinction were admitted, the repetition [of the phrase] would be redundant. Nor is the distinction from a jar the same as the distinction from a cloth; for that would contradict experience. Therefore, the perception of difference is indeed logical.

Furthermore, the postulation of the falsity of even those entities perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) constitutes a "theft of light" precisely because it contradicts valid cognition.

For that which is seen through a *pramāṇa* cannot be sublated by reasoning (*tarka*), since there is a rule that what contradicts perception and the other means of knowledge is necessarily a fallacy of reasoning (*tarkābhāsa*). Even the cognition of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell is considered an error solely because it is contradicted by a stronger perception, not merely by reasoning.

If perception were sublated by mere reasoning, then since the earth-ness of the four elements—such as earth—is not perceived [as distinct from their nature], even earth would lack earth-ness. Therefore, one should not assume that what is perceived is illusory based on mere reasoning alone. Consequently, because the reasoning that seeks to negate all difference contradicts all Śruti, Smṛti, perception, and inference, it is nothing but a fallacy.

Nor can it be said that there is no difference in the ultimate sense, yet that difference exists on the conventional level; for there is no evidence for its being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. For one who argues that the manifestation of the non-existent is impossible, does this manifestation of the non-existent occur or not? If it did not occur, then the non-existent has not been refuted. If it did occur, then [the claim of impossibility] is likewise not established. Furthermore, the distinction of the non-existent cannot be known without the cognition of it.

Nor is the silver-nature in the nacre something distinct from the real, because of the experience: "It was only non-existent silver that appeared. Nor does its appearance imply an absence of non-existence; for error consists precisely in a misapprehension, namely, the cognition of existence in what is non-existent and the cognition of non-existence in what is existent.

Nor should it be said that there is no cognition even when the object is non-existent (*asat*), for you yourself accept that the ultimate reality of the indescribable (*anirvacanīya*) is perceived precisely as something non-existent. Furthermore, that [indescribability] itself cannot be indescribable, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the first [instance of] the indescribable were not established, the second would not be established either; thus, the very root [of your position] would be destroyed. Moreover, if the silver were indescribable, a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*) in the form "this silver is indescribable" would arise. The word "false" (*mithyā*), however, denotes non-existence.

Furthermore, there is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that there exists something distinct from both being and non-being; moreover, that position contradicts experience, since both being and non-being are experienced by everyone. Therefore, because the indefinable (anirvacanīya) does not exist, because the perception of the non-existent is not admitted, and because difference is perceived—thereby necessitating its existence—the state of non-duality (advitīyatva) is untenable.

And how can the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), established by the *śruti*, be refuted? Furthermore, if the *śruti* is a speaker of falsehood, how can the oneness (*aikya*) [of the two] possess reality? Moreover, how can those who speak thus be considered proponents of the Veda (*vedavādin*)? For by accepting the falsity of what is declared in the Veda, even the Buddhists and others would indeed be non-proponents of the Veda (*avedavādin*). Therefore, the great purport (*mahātātparya*) of all the scriptures is precisely that Viṣṇu is the supreme among all.

And how can it be appropriate for all the Śrutis to have their purport in the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? Because that would contradict all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance, there is a contradiction with experience. Indeed, no one has the experience, "I am omniscient, the Lord of all, free from suffering, and free from defects. On the contrary, there is an experience to the opposite effect. Nor is this [latter] experience false, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition to the contrary. Furthermore, there is no scripture whatsoever regarding non-duality; rather, all scriptures concern duality. To illustrate:
The instruction "Thou art That" is given nine times along with illustrative examples. Nor is this an instruction regarding non-difference [merely figurative].
"Just as a bird tied by a string... O Somya, all these beings have Being (Sat) as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. (1)

"Just as, my dear, bees prepare honey by bringing together the juices of trees from various directions and reducing them to a single unity, and as those juices there do not distinguish themselves, thinking, 'I am the juice of this tree,' or 'I am the juice of that tree'—even so, my dear, these rivers, having reached Being, do not know, 'We shall become merged in Being.
Whatever they are here—whether tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gadfly, or mosquito—that is what they become. (2)

"Just as, my dear, these rivers flow eastward in the front and westward in the rear, and they enter only the ocean from the ocean; they become the ocean itself. Just as there they find no distinction and do not know, 'I am this one,' or 'I am that one,' even so, my dear, all these creatures, having come from Being, do not know, 'We are coming from Being.
Whatever they are here—whether tiger, lion, wolf, boar, worm, moth, gadfly, or mosquito—that is what they become. (3)
This very tree, pervaded by the living self (jīva-ātman), stands drinking deeply and rejoicing. When the living self leaves one of its branches, that branch withers.

"Bring a fruit of the banyan tree," [the father said]. "Here it is, venerable sir," [the son replied]. "Break it open," [the father said]. "It is broken, venerable sir. "What do you see there? "These seeds, as it were, are very small, venerable sir. "Now, my dear, break one of these," [the father said]. "It is broken, venerable sir. "What do you see there? "Nothing at all, venerable sir. He said to him: "My dear, that subtle essence which you do not perceive—of this very subtle essence, my dear, this great banyan tree stands. || 5 ||

"Place this salt in water and do not come to me until morning. He did exactly so. He said to him, "My dear, bring that salt which you placed in the water last evening. Having searched for it, he did not find it, for it had completely dissolved. [The father said,] "Taste it from the surface, my dear. "How is it? "It is salt. "Taste it from the middle. "How is it? "It is salt. "Taste it from the bottom. "How is it? "It is salt. "Having set this aside, then come to me. He did exactly so, and [the father said] that [salt] was indeed always there.
"It comes together. He said to him, "In this very place, my dear, you do not perceive this subtle essence; it is indeed right here."
"Just as, my dear, if they were to bring a man from Gandhāra with his eyes bound and then leave him in a place where there are no people," ||| 7 ||
Now, when his speech merges into the mind, the mind into the breath, the breath into heat, and the heat into the supreme deity, then he does not perceive.

"O Somya, they bring a man, seized by the hand, saying: 'He has stolen; he has committed theft; heat the axe for him! If he is the doer of that deed, then he makes himself false. Being intent on falsehood, having concealed himself with falsehood, he grasps the heated axe; he is burned and then slain. But if he is not the doer of that deed, then he makes himself true."

Being true to his word, he conceals himself by means of truth and takes up the axe; he is not burned and is then released. "In this very same way, my dear, a man who has a teacher knows," [it is said] even in the nine instances, because difference alone is expressed through the illustrations.

For there is no identity between a bird and its tether, various tree juices, a river and the ocean, a living being and a tree, the individual soul and the Pradhāna, salt and water, a person from Gandhāra and another person, the ignorant one and the controller of the vital breaths, or a thief and the one who seizes him.

Having attained Being, they do not know, "We are attaining Being"; having come from Being, they do not know, "We are coming from Being. Because of their failure to recognize the distinction—thinking here, "I am a tiger" or "I am a lion"—and because of the statement regarding the resulting harm, [it follows that they are not liberated].

For there is no identity between one who has come from a house and one who has entered that same house. Even in the passage, "They go from the ocean back into the ocean itself; they become the ocean itself," it is precisely difference that is being stated; otherwise, the designation would have been "they become the ocean. Therefore, the meaning is that the rivers come from the ocean and enter it, yet the ocean remains as it is, and these [rivers] do not attain the state of being the ocean.

For it is not logical that distinct river-water atoms should attain identity with ocean atoms; if that were so, then two or three people who have entered a great assembly would become one with it. And that is not logical, because their difference is perceived. In the phrase "he becomes merged into his own (svam apīto bhavati)," the word "his own" (sva) is a designation for the Supreme Self. This is because of the Sūtra, "And by his own self in the latter two," where the Self is called "his own" (sva) due to its sovereignty, and this [individual] is so called because it has expanded from that [Self].
Because he is full of all virtues, this Lord Viṣṇu is the imperishable Brahman.

Thus it is said in the *Paramopaniṣad*. In the phrase "he has entered" (*apītaḥ*), there is merely a sense of entry; this is because of the use of the accusative case in the word "his own" (*svam*). If the intention were to express a state of complete unification, the instrumental case "by himself" (*svena*) would have been used.
Just as a bird might enter its own nest, so too [the individual soul] enters the Lord.
And [it is said]: "The individual soul (jīva) always departs, even while being distinct [from the Self], both in deep sleep and in liberation. And also:

"In this very way, my dear, this mind (manas), having flown in every direction and finding no resting place elsewhere, takes refuge in the vital breath (prāṇa) alone. Here too, "mind" refers to the individual soul and "vital breath" to the Supreme Self, because those two alone were the subject under discussion in the passage beginning, "When this person sleeps...

Furthermore, the individual person (pudgala) is designated as "mind" (manas) because of its capacity for thinking (manana), and as "hell" (niraya) because it swallows [the consequences of] its own actions.
"And because he follows after karma and the latent tendencies (anuśaya), he is remembered as one who follows along with the transmigrating beings," so it is said in the *Paramopaniṣad*.
Also: "Because he causes the departure of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and because of his goodness (sādhutva), this Hari is remembered as 'Sat' (Being).

Furthermore, in the passage, "O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support," it is likewise perceived that there is indeed a distinction [between them].

"Because He is the creator, because He is the support, and because He establishes each and every one of the liberated souls, Viṣṇu is considered the all-pervading Lord, distinct from the transmigrating soul. Furthermore, in the passage: "Having entered by means of the individual soul (jīva-ātman), let me manifest names and forms; thus, having entered as the individual soul, He remains drinking, rejoicing, and delighting," the Supreme Self is denoted by the word *jīva*. For scripture states: "The name of the Blessed One Aniruddha is *jīva*"; and it is said that Viṣṇu is called *jīva* because He constantly sustains the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Having entered, he likewise enters the body, both the stationary and the moving.
And the omnipresent [Self], preceded by the tripartition of the great elements,
perpetually causes the transmigrating being— who is characterized by difference— to wander.

"Therefore, even when he has reached the state of a tree, he rejoices eternally, though he is not [in that form]. And because consciousness was already established previously by the statements, "That fire thought," "Those waters thought," and "These three deities," it is not logical that the transmigrating soul (saṃsārī) should enter again as expressed in the phrase, "By this living self (jīva-ātman). Therefore, in that context, the Supreme Self alone is denoted by the word *jīva*.
Even in the passage, "Pervaded by the living self, he remains drinking deeply and rejoicing," that which is designated by the word *jīva* is indeed the Supreme Self.

The transmigrating being (saṃsārī), indeed, drinks deeply and rejoices; for it is not fitting that anything other than consciousness should possess joy, enjoyment, and so forth. Furthermore, the body is the locus of pleasure and the body is the locus of pain.
They say that this [body] which has been introduced as insentient is the object of experience, while the conscious embodied self is the experiencer thereof. Thus it is stated in the *Mahābhārata*.

In the passage, "Verily, this [body] dies when deprived of the *jīva*; the *jīva* does not die," the word *jīva* also refers to the Supreme. For it is not logically possible for a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*) to be the primary sustainer of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). Furthermore, as stated in the verse, "A man is said to be dead when his body has been abandoned by Brahman," and in the passage, "That subtle essence (*aṇiman*), my dear, which you do not perceive—verily, my dear, from this very subtle essence this great banyan tree exists," the Supreme alone is denoted by the term *aṇiman*.
This is because it has been stated: "That which is this subtle essence (aṇimā)—all this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self, and you are That, O Śvetaketu.

However, in the case of the grains, because of the use of the feminine gender in the phrase "these grains are, as it were, subtle" (aṇvyas) and because of the word "as it were" (iva), they do not possess the state of being the subtle essence. Furthermore, one does not fail to perceive them.
The term "aitadātmyam" means "having that as its self," and the word "Self" (ātman) refers exclusively to the Supreme.

In the aphorisms "The abode of heaven, earth, and so forth [is Brahman], because of its own word," "Not the inferred [Pradhāna], because of the absence of its word," and "And [it is] not the vital breath," the Lord Vyāsa has declared that because of the word *ātman*—which is a synonym for "its own word" (*svaśabda*) in the passage "Know Him alone as the one Self"—neither Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) nor the individual soul (*jīva*) is denoted, but rather the Supreme alone. Therefore, the word *ātman* is primary in reference to Him alone:
"Because He is all-pervading (*ātata*), because He is the knower (*mātṛ*), the Supreme Hari is the Self (*ātman*)."
The others are merely reflections of the self, for they do not possess those qualities in their full extent.

Thus it is stated in the *Paramopaniṣad*. Regarding the passage, "He does not know the splendor in the Supreme Deity," it is said that when the Supreme One swallows his vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, he does not know; when He gives them back, then he knows. This expresses His very subjection [to Him].
When the Lord gives back the vital breaths, then the entire world of sentient beings [awakens].
And as it is said: "When the instruments [of perception] are swallowed, one knows nothing at all.

Furthermore, in the case of the statements "He has taken" or "He has committed theft," since it is only another's property that can be stolen, this is an illustration of difference alone. One who considers the Supreme Self, which is distinct, to be himself is indeed a thief; for one does not become a thief by abandoning what belongs to oneself.
This so-called "oneness" (aikātmya) is something that only the unskilled would speak of.
Without understanding the true reality from the treatises, people likewise [speak] out of the strength of their own arguments.
Overcome by desire and anger, fallen under the sway of egoism,
and failing to understand the true meaning of the scriptures, these enemies of the teachings act contrary to the scriptures.
Those who steal the Veda are joyless, undeveloped in mind, and inauspicious;
they perceive only defects and do not apply themselves to virtues.
For those whose bodies are darkness, darkness alone is their ultimate resort;
for they are different from him by nature, by birth, by scripture, and by purpose.
"How could there be a connection such as 'I am he' when they are not joined? thus it is said in the *Mokṣadharma*.
"Just as a bird and its string, just as the juices of various trees, just as rivers and the ocean, and just as pure water and salt."
Just as a thief and his victim, and just as two men in a marketplace,
so too are the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) distinct and always characterized by difference;
nevertheless, because of His subtle form, Hari is not perceived apart from the individual soul.
To those of dull vision, even the Impeller appears as distinct;
having understood the difference between the two, one is liberated, otherwise one is bound.
And thus it is said in the Paramopaniṣad:
"He is the impeller of all living beings, and He is the one who impels their vital breaths and intellects;
that Viṣṇu is distinct from those who wander in saṃsāra—he who, being of deluded intellect, does not know Him."
"One considers the self to be the leader of the body, senses, vital breath, and intellect;
therefore, one always follows the path of saṃsāra for both the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśa).
Having known the supreme distinction between them, one is liberated; otherwise, one is bound. Thus it is said.

"Having studied all the Vedas, the high-minded one, considering himself a learned scholar, went forth arrogant. Thus, by demonstrating that he was dependent on another who possessed qualities such as being a learned scholar—thereby dispelling his arrogance—the state of being established in That (the Self) is taught here. Furthermore, even the doctrines established by other disputants, such as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existence alone," are refuted.
"The deluded, regarding sacrifices and public works as the highest, do not know any other higher good."
And this [view] is obtained through a failure to understand the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of such scriptural passages.
Furthermore, it has been shown [by us]: "That which some unskilled people call 'monism' (*aikātmya*).
And the narration of creation, beginning with "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedamagra āsīt*), is for the purpose of making known that very [non-duality].
And the cognition of all through a single cognition occurs because of its predominance, some degree of similarity, and its causality; it is not, however, because anything other than that is false.

For false cognition does not arise from the cognition of reality; indeed, one who knows mother-of-pearl is not called one who knows silver, because of the contradiction between those two cognitions. One who knows mother-of-pearl is indeed one who knows "this is not silver," for if he were a knower of silver, he would not be a knower of mother-of-pearl. For one who knows a thing cannot simultaneously be a knower of its absence; moreover, the fact that the cognition of the absence of a thing is preceded by the cognition of that thing is observed elsewhere precisely because of its existence. If that [existence] were not admitted, even that [cognition of absence] would not be tenable.

Indeed, there is the designation of something subordinate as "known" based on the knowledge of the primary thing; for example, when the principal persons [of a village] have been known, summoned, or destroyed, one designates the village as "known," "summoned," or "destroyed. Furthermore, when the father, who is the cause, is known, it is said that the son is known; the designation is "I know him, for he is his son. Similarly, in this case as well, there is the statement "all this was created by Him," and so forth.

And because of similarity, there is knowledge from one [thing]. That very similarity is intended here as well, as in the passage beginning, "O dear one, by means of a single lump of clay, all that is made of clay would be known. Otherwise, the words "one" (*eka*) and "lump" (*piṇḍa*) would be redundant; for the point would be complete simply by saying "by means of clay being known," since other things made of clay are not identical in essence to that single lump of clay. Rather, they possess only similarity to it.

"O dear one, just as by means of a single iron ornament everything made of iron would be known; or, O dear one, just as by means of a single nail-cutter everything made of black iron would be known"—statements such as these would also be rendered meaningless. For that which consists of a single ornament is not something else made of iron, nor is everything made of black iron identical with a single nail-cutter.

Regarding the passage, "The modification is a verbal handle, a mere name; 'clay' alone is the truth," the meaning of the Śruti is that the modification is a verbal handle—that is, a name produced by speech—and that the eternal name, such as "clay" and so forth, is indeed the truth; this is purely a Vedic statement. Furthermore, the term *vācārambhaṇa* is not well-known in the sense of "falsity. Moreover, the interpretation "merely a verbal handle" involves the assumption of words not actually heard in the text. In that case, the word *nāmadheya* ("name") would be redundant. Therefore, nowhere is the falsity of the world asserted.
"The wise, the thoughtful, the all-encompassing one has himself ordained things according to their true nature for eternal years.
"Whatever he intends is indeed truth, not in vain; he is the winner of desirable wealth and the giver.
All is truth for you two, O Maghavans; even the waters do not violate your vow."
I shall now proclaim the great and true deeds of this Great One, the Truth of truth: "This world, such as it is, proceeds without beginning or end; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
It has never been otherwise at any time or for anyone, nor will it ever become so."

"The ignorant say this world is unreal, for they do not know the supreme power of Hari. That Great Soul, whose actions are true, having created this world of such a true form, Himself became its reality. "They say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord."
"Arising from neither self nor other, what else could it have as its cause but desire?
Holding fast to this view, those of ruined souls and small intellects, performers of fierce deeds, arise for the destruction of the world, harmful to themselves. And so forth.
The world’s similarity to a dream and so forth is due to its nature of impermanence, mutability, dependence, and the like; it is not, however, because it is to be sublated by awakening.
"Since all this is perceived by Viṣṇu, the omniscient one, therefore this [universe] is incapable of knowing him; rather, it is indeed subject to his command," so it is said in the Paramopaniṣad.
Since the world is emanated by wisdom, it is therefore composed of illusion;
since it is followed by this [wisdom], it is for that reason called "unreal."
Furthermore, although it cannot be subverted by awakening, it is indeed eternal in its continuous flow;
thus the supreme Veda is called "A," and by that, this world is true.
"Because its nature is dependent upon that [the Self], it is said to be unreal;
yet that omnipresent Lord is the reality of reality, just as the sun is to the rainbow. Thus it is said.
"His secret doctrine (upaniṣad) is 'the truth of truth. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth, and he is their truth.
And:
"He is known as Mahāmāyā, as Avidyā, as Niyati, and as Mohinī."
"O Infinite One, your will is described as both primordial nature (prakṛti) and latent impression (vāsanā)."

Nature (*prakṛti*) is so called because it brings about excellence, since it perfumes (*vāsayet*) through latent impressions (*vāsanā*); "A" refers to Hari, and his [powers] are designated as knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Having said 'māyā,' because it is pre-eminent, that which is called *mayā* is indeed pre-eminent. Of Viṣṇu, there is only one [reality], namely *prajñapti* (consciousness), which is expressed by these various words.
For Hari is of the nature of *prajñapti*, and she is characterized by her own bliss. Thus it is said.
Indeed, all the Vedas teach that Hari is distinct from everything;
that distinction consists of His independence, omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
This distinction is His very essential nature (*svarūpa*), and this exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is His essential nature itself.
"Since this word 'own' (sva) is employed for the purpose of excluding everything else,

the Śruti— through such passages as 'Not this, not this' (neti neti)— speaks of Viṣṇu's very state of being excluded from all else; therefore, there is no doubt that all other [scriptures] also declare this."
And thus says the Nārāyaṇa-śruti:
"I am Brahman"; "He who is I, he is that; he who is that, he is I";
"That person who is yonder in the sun, I am he; I am indeed he."
The passage beginning with "Thus, etc. refers to the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). [It says]:
"That which is here in the person and that which is yonder in the sun are one. "Aham" is Brahman; "I have come there" is its secret name (*upaniṣad*); "Aham" (I).

Hari is eternally proclaimed by the name "I" (aham) because He is never to be abandoned; and You are designated as "this one" (asau) due to being the counter-correlative, while He is also called "that one" (saḥ) because of His transcendence. Thus, all the case-inflections of the word "we" (asmad) refer to Hari, the inner controller of all.
All case-endings (*vibhakti*) belonging to the word *yuṣmad*,
as well as all numbers (*vacana*) belonging to the word *yuṣmad*,
function at all times independently, even when [the referent] is excluded from everything else.

"However, due to that connection, all verbal forms (tiṅpadāni) apply metaphorically to individual souls (jīva) because of their connection with Him, and even to insentient things (acit) because of their connection with them.
Therefore, Viṣṇu alone is omnipresent; yet, through differentiation, He becomes manifold."
Thus says the Nārāyaṇa-śruti:
"Know that knowledge to be *sāttvika* by which one perceives the single, immutable reality in all beings, undivided within the divided."
Thus says the word of the Blessed One.
And difference is not unreal;
for they truly rejoice after him, celebrating the gift of the generous god who bestows wealth.
True is that majesty of his; his power is manifest at the sacrifices in the kingdom of the wise.
True is the Self, true is the individual soul, true is the distinction—true is the distinction, true is the distinction!
Not to be spoken of as "mine," not to be spoken of as "mine," not to be spoken of as "mine"!

"For the Self is indeed supremely independent, all-knowing, omnipotent, possessing supreme bliss, and the highest; whereas the individual soul (jīva) is subject to it, possessing little knowledge, little power, afflicted, and insignificant"—from such scriptural passages as these. Nor is this [distinction] merely a relative truth. "He who knows Him hidden in the cave, in the highest heaven... [and so forth].
"He attains all desires together with the wise Brahman—having approached this Self consisting of bliss, moving through these worlds at will and assuming forms at will, he remains singing this Sāman:
'One part of him, having thrived, sits nourishing the Ṛks; another sings the Gāyatra upon the Śakvarī verses.'"
Brahmā indeed speaks the knowledge of all that has been born; he alone measures out the proper proportions of the sacrifice.
"Having attained the highest light, he manifests in his own true form.
There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing, with women, or with chariots, or with kinsmen, or with non-kinsmen."

"But where everything has become the Self alone for him, by what and whom should he see? By what and whom should he smell? By what and whom should he know? By what should he know that by which one knows all this? O friend, by what should one know the Knower?
"As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it," so the wise man, having shaken off both merit and demerit, free from stain, attains the supreme equality.
"This is the bridge to immortality.
Friends endowed with eyes and ears have become unequal in their mental speed;
some reach only to the mouth, others to the armpits, while still others appear as if they have bathed in the very heart.
Taking refuge in the Lord, those liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra remain there,
enjoying their desired pleasures up to the level of Brahmā, each succeeding one surpassing the previous.

And so forth, because of scriptural texts concerning difference after liberation. For instance, there is the word of the Blessed One: "Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature; even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer."
"Excluding the activity of the world," and "because of the context and because of being non-proximate.

This is because the non-cessation of its attributes has been introduced [in the passage]: "Verily, this Self is imperishable, O Maitreyī, its nature is indestructible. Furthermore, in this very context, the Blessed One led [Maitreyī] to the end of her delusion by stating that "there is no consciousness after death" is a defect, as it is a negation of consciousness.

For where "all has become the Self alone for him, then by what and whom should he see?"—this is indeed a negation. Indeed, the absence of enjoyment is not required, nor is the lack of cognition on the part of the knower, as indicated by: "By what, O Maitreyī, should one know the Knower?"
That which is to be known as "I" alone is celebrated as the individual soul (jīva);
it is that which experiences suffering and happiness, and it is the recipient of both bondage and liberation.

And thus says the supreme Śruti: "For one submerged in ignorance regarding the Supreme, what could be more painful? (Mokṣadharma). And also: "But there is no second to that. This means that when one does not perceive that Brahman as duality, for him there is no second; this is stated because of the supplementary passage: "Whatever else one might see as distinct from that," and because of the reason: "For there is no loss of the vision of the Seer."

In the passage, "The actions and the self consisting of consciousness all become one in the supreme, imperishable [Brahman]," this "becoming one" (ekībhāva) refers either to identity of thought or to identity of location, in view of their respective forms as they exist in the ocean of milk and so forth.
[As it is said: "Through desire, my desire has come from the heart; this [desire] is from death."
"Whatever is dear to them, let that come toward me through these [words].
My intellect shall become favorable to the realization of Brahman and intent upon liberation;
therefore, for the most part, favorability remains with me even now."
This is because of such scriptural passages as: "By which the seers, whose desires are fulfilled, ascend to where that supreme treasure of Truth is," and "He approaches this Self consisting of bliss.

If the intention were identity of essential nature (*svarūpa-ekya*), the statement "the works and the one consisting of consciousness" would not be appropriate; for even in that view, there is no identity of the works with Brahman in the state of liberation.

If the intention were [merely] cessation, then since even the fifteen *kalās* would be equal [in that regard], the statement of the departure of other *kalās*—namely, "The fifteen *kalās* have gone, as well as all the deities into their respective deities"—and the subsequent description of the unification of the *karmas* and the *vijñānātman* would be purposeless, as there would be no distinction [between them]. Furthermore, there is no conventional usage of the unification of silver with mother-of-pearl once the [erroneous] cognition has ceased. Moreover, the statement of its abiding in the supreme imperishable (*pare 'vyaye*) indicates a state of difference; otherwise, the designation would have been "they become the Supreme itself."
The supreme identity of the individual soul (jīva) with the Supreme, however, is merely a conformity of intellect (buddhisārūpya),
or it is residence in the same place, depending on the location of manifestation.
"There is no identity of essential nature for him, even when liberated, because of his difference [from the Lord].
Difference consists in [the soul's] limitedness and dependence versus [the Lord's] sovereignty and fullness. Thus says the Supreme Scripture (*paramaśruti*).
And also: "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman itself," and so forth.
It is like the saying: "Even a Śūdra becomes a Brāhmaṇa by worshipping a Brāhmaṇa with devotion. The meaning is that he becomes expanded (bṛṃhita).
For one who merely worships a Brāhmaṇa does not himself become a Brāhmaṇa.
[As it is said: "All individual souls (jīvas) are indeed Brahman; those who attain liberation become the Supreme Brahman."

"Prakṛti is the supreme Brahman, the supreme Mahat, the infallible; yet she is neither liberated from Him, nor does she ever attain the glory of Viṣṇu. He alone is independent and possessed of perfect, auspicious qualities"—thus says the Supreme Śruti.

"O Hari, you alone are that absolute state of liberation (kaivalya), which is your true nature— beyond all measure, increasing through your own body, and whose greatness no one can fully attain, even by means of the powers of Brahmā, Īśāna, and others. Thus it is said.
Just as all rays of light, though existing separately by their own natures throughout the day, merge into the sun of great splendor; even so,
the entities called individual souls (jīvas), which are indeed Brahman, merge into the Supreme Brahman.
In liberation, they remain indeed separate; for others, there is no perception [of them].
This is declared to be their dissolution, never an identity of essential nature.
Thus says the Nārāyaṇa-śruti.
Therefore, the identity of the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (paramātman) is indeed contrary to all scriptures,
and likewise contrary to all reasoning.

First of all, the doctrine of a single soul (ekajīvavāda) is not tenable. Furthermore, if everything were imagined by the ignorance of a single individual, then for one who knows that "all this is imagined," the instruction of disciples and others would be untenable; for having ascertained that "this is a dream," one does not strive for the sake of a son or inheritance within that dream. It is only because of the lack of knowledge regarding the dream-state that one strives within a dream. Nor is it reasonable to ascertain that "this is imagined by [my] ignorance" simply because many things are being perceived.

In a dream, however, because only one [the waking state] remains after awakening, there is certainty; but that is not the case here. If it were accepted that "each of those [states] is to be understood as being thus," then since no conceptual differentiation is possible regarding a real entity (*vastu*), it would simply follow that it is non-imagined (*akalpita*). Yet, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the claim that "it is to be understood in such a way. If it were accepted that it is imagined by the ignorance of the disciple, then, since he himself becomes the teacher, it would be imagined by him alone; thus, the correct mastery of the text would become a cause of harm.

And there would be no liberation for anyone; for upon the acquisition of the [scriptural] texts, it would follow that those very texts are merely imagined through the ignorance of that single soul (ekajīva). Furthermore, if that single soul were a proponent of duality (*bhedavādī*), then because of his firm adherence to that [duality], there would never be a cessation of duality, and thus no one would attain liberation. Consequently, since things exist exactly as they are imagined, that same [eternal hell] would result for the proponents of the single soul (*ekajīvavādin*) who imagine such a state. Moreover, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the claim that "the entire universe is imagined through the ignorance of a single soul. As it is said: "If the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) existed, it would undoubtedly cease."
This duality is mere illusion; from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is non-dual.

And this is the meaning of that [verse]: if this manifold world (prapañca) were to exist—that is, if it were to come into being or arise—then it would cease; but since it does not cease, it is therefore indeed beginningless.

The manifold (prapañca) is a fivefold, preeminent differentiation. And this is not non-existent, because it is "mere illusion" (māyāmātra). "Illusion" (māyā) is the wisdom of the Blessed One; that which has her as its protector (māna-trāṇa-kartṛ) is "mere illusion. Because it is known and protected by the Supreme Lord, duality is not imagined through delusion—this is the meaning. For there is no delusion in the Lord. To the question, "How then is there the designation 'non-dual in all things'?", he says: "Non-dual from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ)."

For non-duality (advaitatva) is with respect to the ultimate reality (paramārtha). The meaning is that the object which is superior to everything is one alone; otherwise, the statement "non-duality of all entities" would be redundant. If it were said that among all entities this one alone possesses non-duality, it would merely be stating its lack of a superior. Furthermore, there is a state of being superior to all these other entities. Moreover, from the remainder of the passage—"If it were imagined by anyone, then conceptual construction (vikalpa) would cease"—it is understood that this [reality] is not something imagined.

If one accepts the meaning "it ceases," then the statements "it would cease" and "it would be known" (vidyeta) as hypothetical consequences (*prasaṅga*), as well as the use of the word *yadi* ("if"), would be inappropriate. Furthermore, if one does not accept that "it would be known" means "it arises," then because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*)—namely, that whatever exists ceases—it would be inappropriate to say "it would cease. Therefore, this sentence refers to the beginningless and eternal nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Consequently, he says: "This discourse is for the sake of instruction; duality does not exist when [the Truth] is not known. The meaning is: "Duality does not exist only when [the Truth] is not known"; that is, duality does not exist only from the perspective of the ignorant.

The distinction between the individual soul and the Lord, as well as the distinction between the insentient and the Lord; the mutual distinction among individual souls, and likewise the distinction between the insentient and the individual soul.
This manifold world, consisting of the fivefold division of difference, is mutually insentient;
it is indeed real and beginningless. If it were to have a beginning, it would meet with destruction;
yet this world does not undergo destruction, nor is it imagined through delusion.
If that which is imagined were to cease here, it would not cease;
therefore, the view that "duality does not exist" belongs to the ignorant.
"For this is the opinion of the wise; it is measured and protected by Viṣṇu.
Therefore, it is declared as 'Truth' (Satya), for Hari alone is the Supreme. Thus says the Parama-Śruti.
And in the Maitreyī-Śākhā:

"Next, the obstacles to knowledge. Having said this, [the text continues]: "Furthermore, one should not dwell with those others who, by means of fallacious arguments, fallacious examples, and deceptive nets of illusion, seek to stand against the Vedic teachings; for these are thieves manifest in public, leading away from heaven," so it is said.

"Deluded by the sprouts of the doctrine of non-self (*nairātmya*) and by fallacious examples and reasons, the world does not recognize that which is another form of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus [it is said].

The doctrine that nothing whatsoever belongs to the self is the doctrine of *nairātmya* (non-self). If the world were merely imagined through delusion, it would not require a real world as its basis; for a delusion does not arise in the absence of a real mother-of-pearl, a real silver, and the similarity between the two. Even in a dream, the world—which exists in the mind in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)—is perceived as being external, though it is indeed real. Furthermore, there is indeed a similarity between the body and the self, such as their occupying the same location.

Even in cases such as "the conch is yellow" or "the sky is blue," the yellowness and so forth do indeed exist elsewhere; furthermore, there is some degree of similarity between the conch and so on, such as their common possession of substantiality (*dravyatva*). Therefore, nowhere does an error occur without two real objects that resemble one another.

Furthermore, the delusion of the non-self in the self has never been observed anywhere; for no one is seen who is deluded such that they think, "I am not I. It is asserted by them that this entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is precisely the delusion of the non-self in the self. If, however, one were to imagine the delusion of the self in the non-self without that [delusion of the non-self in the self], then the non-self would have to be real. In that case, when imagining non-duality, it would follow that only the non-self exists and not the self.

Furthermore, if the world were of the nature of ignorance regarding the Self, it would not be perceived as distinct from the Self; for in an illusion, silver is never seen as distinct from mother-of-pearl. Nor is a single thing ever seen as manifold simultaneously in an illusion. Moreover, an illusion of difference within the Self has never been observed anywhere, nor has a difference produced by a false limiting adjunct (*mithyopādhi*) ever been seen anywhere. Furthermore, neither knowledge nor ignorance is ever seen to be falsely imagined; rather, in an illusion, it is only the object thereof that is otherwise. This position is contradicted by such infinite arguments as these. I shall desist here, lest the work become too voluminous.

Nor is there any fault in accepting [the self] as real. Even in the position of those who maintain that there are many jīvas, these very faults would arise if they were to accept that difference is illusory. For even according to them, their plurality is produced by illusory limiting adjuncts (upādhis). Furthermore, a difference produced by an illusory adjunct is never observed anywhere. Since it consists of the imagination of the non-self within the Self, an illusory adjunct is simply not tenable. Even an illusionary creation is seen only when something else similar to it already exists, and it occurs only by depending upon some substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) endowed with similarity, such as substantiality and so forth.
Furthermore, without two similar real entities as a basis,
no delusion occurs anywhere, even in cases such as dreams and illusions.

The conceptualization of external objects within mental impressions is like a dream-delusion; and within the realm of māyā, it is like [the perception of] real entities such as the agent, the body, and so forth.

"The conceptualization of [the Lord] as possessing a fourfold army and so forth is held to be an illusion. Since the universe is not conceptually constructed by such an illusion, it is therefore dependent upon the power of Viṣṇu. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmavaivarta*.
Furthermore, the Lord is not seen as a world-illusion like that of Māyā.

"Because he always sees this [world], let it be understood that it is not an illusion. And: "A false perception can never occur for one who possesses direct vision; Viṣṇu, the seer of all, perceives everything directly, therefore that [world] is not false. And:

Furthermore, if it is held that the one Brahman alone transmigrates and is liberated due to the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then because transmigrating beings exist at all times, Brahman would always be nothing but a transmigrator. Consequently, even the attainment of its true nature would not be liberation, since it would remain eternally connected with limiting adjuncts. Nor can it be argued that there is no connection with limiting adjuncts for the pure [Brahman], for if that which is already connected to an adjunct were to undergo a further connection with an adjunct, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor can it be said that it is connected by that very same relation, as that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*).

For this reason as well, a false limiting adjunct (*mithyopādhi*) is not tenable. The establishment of a false limiting adjunct depends upon the establishment of ignorance (*ajñāna*), because falsity cannot be established without ignorance. Nor can ignorance be established without a false limiting adjunct, because only that which is distinct from a false limiting adjunct is characterized by ignorance. If the pure [Self] itself were ignorant, it would follow that even the liberated one is ignorant; for ignorance would then be intrinsic (*svābhāvika*), real (*satya*), and entail the existence of a second entity (*sadvitīyatva*). Furthermore, since an intrinsic nature is admitted to be non-terminating, it would follow that ignorance is never terminated. That a real thing is non-terminating is their position. Therefore, there is a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatā*).

If ignorance is established, then the false limiting adjunct (*mithyopādhi*) is established; if the false limiting adjunct is established, then the individual soul (*jīva*) is established; and if the individual soul is established, then ignorance, which has that soul as its locus, is established—this constitutes a circular argument (*cakraka*). Nor is it logical to say that the pure [Self] itself is ignorant through delusion; for if ignorance is established, then delusion is established, and if delusion is established, then ignorance is established—thus there is mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*).
[As it is said: "However many moments exist, combined, in the past and the future; however many atoms exist, in the past and the future..."
Furthermore, the multitudes of individual souls are infinitely greater than even that, according to the *Vatsa-śruti*: "There is no end to the transmigrating beings in our doctrine;
for even within the space of a single atom, there are infinite multitudes of living beings."
"Indeed, even though they are gross, they exist by the power of the Lord alone because of His subtlety.
And from the Skanda Purāṇa: "By the power of Viśvakarman, infinite heaps of provisions for infinite creatures were established within the assembly hall measuring a thousand yojanas."

Furthermore, the very difficulty of accounting for a false object is not its ornament; for the postulation of falsity regarding an observed object depends upon the strength of perception and the requirement of valid means of knowledge and reasoning. In the absence of these, its reality is established by perception itself.

For when one sees food or other objects of enjoyment, one does not require another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish their reality for the purpose of eating them.
