However, if someone were to say, "This is not food," one would not require another means of valid cognition to determine how this thing, which is being perceived as food, can fail to be food. Furthermore, it is never observed that what is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is sublated by inference (*anumāna*) or other means—apart from scripture (*āgama*)—in a manner more powerful than that perception itself.

In the case of a distant tree, its shortness, and so forth, since the mere lack of clarity in perception is certain, the determination of its length is made through reasoning. For it is established by powerful perception itself that at a distance, perception is dull and its apprehension of dimensions and the like is otherwise;

yet, the falsity of the perception of the world has not been determined by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In particular, no falsity is observed in experience regarding objects such as knowledge and ignorance, pleasure and pain, or the distinction between the self and others.

Therefore, since saṃsāra is real and it is accepted that what is real cannot cease to exist, there would be no liberation. If one were to accept the falsity of something established by experience based on logic alone—without a more powerful experience—then even the self (ātman) would have to be false, because logic accepts the falsity of everything else. Furthermore, to postulate two kinds of reality would involve the fault of conceptual complexity (kalpanā-gaurava). Since an error with the self as its substratum is itself unestablished, it is not logical for the self to be the substratum of such an error. Moreover, if "inexplicability" (durghaṭatva) is considered an ornament rather than a defect, then the falsity of the self, however difficult to establish, would necessarily follow.

This is because even cognition (*pratīti*) is admitted to be an effect of ignorance (*avidyā*), and its "difficult-to-establish" nature (*durghaṭatva*) is considered an ornament [of that ignorance]. Furthermore, since the real requires logical justification (*yuktyapekṣatva*), everything would become contradictory: such as the agency of seeing belonging to jars and other objects, the insentience (*jaḍatva*) of the Self, and the occurrence of error (*bhrama*) as a manifestation (*pratīti*) even in the absence of a seer and without a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

If one accepts the distinction [of the self] based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then just as no distinction is perceived in the enjoyer of pleasure, pain, and so forth, despite the difference in limiting adjuncts such as hands and feet, likewise no distinction would be seen in the enjoyer despite the difference in bodies and the like. Consequently, the pleasure, pain, and so forth residing in all bodies would have to be experienced by a single entity alone.

Furthermore, just as there is no liberation even when a single finger or limb is removed, so too there would be no liberation upon the removal of a single limiting adjunct, because that very self remains connected to infinite other adjuncts. [As it is said:
"Those with raised weapon-bearing arms [are seen] with their own heads fallen, yet their eyes [remain fixed]."

"Even headless trunks (kabandhas) fell their enemies in battle while looking [at them]," according to this statement from the *Mahābhārata*, there is no distinction [between the self and the body] based on disjunction.

Furthermore, does the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) swallow one part of the self or the entire self? If one part is admitted, the self would possess parts; and it is accepted by those [opponents] that what has parts is impermanent. If the entire self is swallowed, the adjunct could not be a differentiator. If one postulates a portion created by the adjunct, then since that [portion] is created by the adjunct, there is the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśrayatva*). If another adjunct is postulated, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Nor does a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika-bheda*) arise for Īśvara from [the fact that] Brahman is all-pervading; for a distinction based on limiting adjuncts is not observed in the case of two things that are unlimited by space and time.

Furthermore, since the one Īśvara is present in all limiting adjuncts and because such distinction is false, just as there is unity of the enjoyer despite the distinction between hand, foot, and so forth, the state of being the enjoyer of all pleasure, pain, and so on would belong to Īśvara alone.

Since there is no distinction between the two—unconditioned by space and time—due to the absence of any adventitious difference, a pure Brahman distinct from the sufferer cannot be established. Therefore, if transmigratory existence were inherent, there would be no cessation of it at all.

Furthermore, does transmigratory existence (saṃsāra) belong to one who is qualified (viśiṣṭa) or to one who is pure (śuddha)? If it is said to belong to the pure one, there is a self-contradiction. If it is said to belong to the qualified one, is that qualified one something other [than the Self] or the same as it? If it is the same, the aforementioned fault remains. If it is something else, is it eternal or non-eternal? If it is non-eternal, it would simply perish, and there would be no liberation. If it were eternal, then difference (bheda) would be real, because it would persist even in liberation.

If it is accepted that the non-difference of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) exists only when it is differentiated by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), then the essential nature itself would be connected with the adjuncts, and thus its purity would not be established. Furthermore, according to that position, that which has an impure nature can never be pure. Moreover, if one accepts the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the adjuncts, faults such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśrayatva*) have already been stated.

Nor can difference arise from the diversity of beginningless karma; for the establishment of difference caused by adjuncts depends on the establishment of the diversity of karma, and the establishment of that [diversity of karma] depends on the establishment of the former—thus there is mutual dependence.

It is concluded that because it would be corrupted by infinite defects, there would be an excessive proliferation of texts. Therefore, since it contradicts all means of valid cognition, the purport of the Śruti is not on non-difference.

Furthermore, since no indication (lakṣaṇā) is observed for that which is inexpressible by any word, it cannot be known through scripture. Thus, due to its inexpressibility and unknowability, it follows that it is merely a void.

Nor do they assert that [the Self] is knowable by itself, for they maintain that there is a contradiction between the agent and the object. Furthermore, knowledge is never observed to exist without either an object of knowledge—whether it be its own nature or something else—or a knower. Therefore, due to the absence of both knower and known, knowledge itself is likewise a mere void (*śūnyatā*). Consequently, there is no distinction whatsoever from the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). Moreover, knowledge devoid of both knower and known is nowhere observed. And since the difference of God has not been established, it is not logical to claim that the intent of the scriptures is their non-difference.
[Rather, He is] the most excellent of all, free from all defects, filled with all perfections, and distinct from everything.
"All the Vedas are engaged primarily in making known [the Lord] through His distinctness, and not otherwise.
Thus it is stated in the Mahopaniṣad.
Therefore, it is established that the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa is to be known through all the Āgamas as being distinct from everything and as being superior to everything.
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīmad-Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya. 1.
The second chapter:
Brahmā, Śiva, and the gods and others are perishable because their bodies are subject to decay;
Lakṣmī is imperishable because her body is imperishable; and Hari is beyond even her.
By virtue of all their attributes—such as the power of absolute sovereignty, consciousness, and bliss—they are entirely limitless; therefore, they are always subject to His will.
He alone brings about the creation, maintenance, destruction, and concealment of all syllables, as well as their bondage and liberation through the quality of purity (sattva).
The one supreme Hari alone is the light that illumines creation, maintenance, and dissolution; he bestows eternal bliss within the imperishable and grants activity to all.
He has no other creator of the creation and so forth; moreover, He is free from all defects.

Thus says the supreme Śruti. And in the Skanda Purāṇa: "Brahmā, Śeṣa, Suparṇeśa, Śakra, Sūrya, Guha, and others—all these are perishable (kṣara), while Śrī alone is imperishable (akṣara); Hari is beyond even Her."

Whomever I desire, him I make fierce; him I make a Brahman, him a seer of great wisdom. For Rudra, I bend the bow to strike the enemy of prayer with an arrow. I stir up strife against the people; I have entered into heaven and earth.
Tomorrow I shall place his father upon the summit; my womb is within the waters, in the ocean.
That which the sages weave within the ocean, from that supreme Imperishable (akṣara) all creatures have sprung;
from it the source of the world was produced. By means of water he scattered living beings upon the earth; through the plants he entered into men and cattle, and into all moving and unmoving beings.
Beyond this is that which is more subtle than the subtle, higher than the high, and greater than the great.

"That which is one, unmanifest, of infinite forms, the universe, ancient, beyond darkness—that alone they call the Real, that alone they call the Truth; that alone is the supreme Brahman of the seers.
"With oblations, we [approach] the branches of this bountiful god Viṣṇu, the impeller, at his offering."
Behold indeed the greatness of Rudra! You two have traveled along the path rich in nourishment, O Aśvins.
From [his] mind the Moon was born; from [his] eye the Sun was born;
from his mouth Indra and Agni were born; from his breath Vāyu was born.
In the beginning, there was only Nārāyaṇa; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, no Agni and Soma, nor these two, heaven and earth.
There was only Nārāyaṇa; there was neither Brahmā nor Śaṅkara.
Having become a sage, he reflected, and from that these were born.

[This is established] from such scriptural passages as: "Viśva, Hiraṇyagarbha, Agni, Yama, Varuṇa, Rudra, Indra," and "In the beginning, this was indeed only Vāsudeva; there was no Brahmā, nor Śaṅkara; no Indra, Sūrya, Guha, Soma, nor Vināyaka. And so forth.

In the passage "There is nothing higher than Him," the meaning is simply that "there is nothing else [higher]. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the supplementary statement: "By Him this is filled; that which is higher than He is formless and immortal. The word "by Him" (tena), as already mentioned, is referred to by the word "than Him" (tataḥ). Otherwise, it would contradict the statement "there is nothing higher than Him. They indeed declare that Viṣṇu to be supreme, into whom all names enter.
He alone, who is distinct from everything and is eternally one and independent, is considered the supreme Viṣṇu, the possessor of all names.
From such scriptural passages as these, it is stated that names other than His belong only to Him, and not to others;

for in all the Vedas, He alone is described as being without fault, while no such absence of fault is mentioned regarding others at the outset. Furthermore, while the possession of all names is declared for Him in all the Vedas, it is never said of others.
Moreover, the "birth" of Vāsudeva refers to His manifestation and nothing else.
"The birth of the body for others, such as Brahmā and the rest, arises from His impulsion;

the body of Hari is beginningless and eternal, while those of Brahmā and the others are non-eternal. The primary birth belongs to Him, whereas for others it is a manifestation; the birth of Hari is [eternal]. Thus it is stated in the *Parama-śruti*.
Thus ends the second chapter in the *Śrīmad-Viṣṇutattvāvinirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpādācārya. 2.
The third chapter:
He who is free from all defects, the embodied essence of all virtues,
independent, and under whose control all things abide— that Viṣṇu is considered supreme.
Thus it is said in the Paramopaniṣad:
"He who is eternally endowed with all perfect qualities, free from defects, always independent, the supreme Viṣṇu, and devoid of birth, death, and the like."
Nārada said: If Viṣṇu is indeed faultless, how did he take birth among human beings?
How is it that he is seen joined with the afflictions of old age, physical exertion, wounds from weapons, ignorance, and suffering?
O Brahmin, this doubt has been implanted in my heart like a thorn;
it cannot be extracted by other mortals—remove it through the power of your eloquent words.
Brahmā said:
The body of Viṣṇu is not born from the union of male and female;
rather, it is his own eternal form, consisting of flawless consciousness and bliss.
This very birth of Viṣṇu reveals itself in this manner, and no other;
nevertheless, it occurs here and there for the delusion of the asuras and for others as well.
He who possesses pure and excellent qualities may display suffering, ignorance, delusion, and so forth;
yet where is there any sense of smell or such, and where is there ignorance in Him whose independent, inconceivable, and untainted qualities are supreme?
Hari, the Unborn, displays these [defects] only for the sake of making liberation difficult to attain.

"Because of that fault of false vision, they do not attain liberation; rather, by that very same [fault], they go to darkness. Therefore, one should know Viṣṇu as being truly free from defects and manifest in his incarnations. Thus it is said in the *Brahmāṇḍa-purāṇa*.
The qualities, activities, and so forth of Viṣṇu are held to be his very own nature and not something else;
therefore, there is never any mutual difference among them whatsoever.

"Even in its own nature (svarūpa), there is a distinction, just as there is in the state of being that very nature; and even in the absence of difference, all worldly transaction proceeds by means of that [nature] alone. Thus it is said in the Mahopaniṣad.
"Non-difference and identity are just like difference, being devoid of distinction."
Thus, all the qualities of Hari are both expressible and distinct.

If there were a distinction between the non-different and the non-distinct, or between the distinct and the distinct, there would be an infinite regress; thus, the status of being a qualifier cannot be established.
Therefore, without knowing the fundamental connection, one should distinguish the single [reality] of Hari as manifold through the power of fallacious reasoning for the sake of conventional usage.
"Even the distinction is its own essential nature, and it possesses the capacity for self-establishment. Thus it is stated in the *Brahmatarka*.
[The scriptures declare]: "This indeed is that which is without a second," "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity."
And from such scriptural passages as: "Just as water rained upon a mountain peak flows away in various directions, so too one who perceives dharmas as separate runs after those very same things."
In such cases as "the place is everywhere," "the person is independent," and "the constancy of time," their respective relations are exactly like those of things whose nature consists of qualities.
"In the *Brahmatarka* it is said: 'The state of being a possessor of qualities and the state of being an enjoyer of qualities belong to Viṣṇu, and he himself is that [enjoyer].
Having known Viṣṇu as full of all qualities, one is freed from saṃsāra;
enjoying eternal bliss free from suffering, he rejoices in his presence."
And Viṣṇu is the refuge of the liberated, as well as their supreme overlord.
"All these are indeed under His control; He alone is the Lord at all times"—thus says the supreme Śruti. Also:
"He is the bridge to immortality," and "He enjoys all desires together with the wise Brahman," and so forth.
From the King (Indra) up to Śatadhṛti (Brahmā), those who attain liberation do so in an ascending order.

"For they rejoice with all their virtues multiplied a hundredfold"—so indeed says the Śruti. Thus it is established in the Padma Purāṇa that Nārāyaṇa is free from every defect and possesses infinite, perfect attributes. Of Him, three divine forms are declared in the Vedic word; that great splendor (bharga) of the God is truly established as "tat savitur vareṇyam."
Vāyu [composed] the first part based on the words of Rāma; Pṛkṣa the second; and as for that which is the third, consisting of honeyed verses, this work was composed by Keśava.
Salutations to You, Nārāyaṇa, who are independent, the Lord of all, free from defects, whose form is beyond the reach of the senses, my beloved, and perfectly complete.
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīmad-Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya* composed by the venerable teacher Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda. 3.
Thus concludes the Determination of the Reality of Viṣṇu.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
